title: Demonstrate an understanding of diseases, pests and vine abnormalities

lessons.title: Common vine diseases
lessons.html:
Common vine diseases

Most vine diseases are caused by fungi. Fungi spread by spores in wind and water and grow fast in wet, warm or humid weather. Workers walk the vineyard every day, so you are often the first to see a problem. Report it quickly.

DiseaseWhat you see
Downy mildewYellow, oily-looking spots on top of leaves; white, fluffy growth under the leaf; bunches can turn brown and shrivel. Worst after spring and summer rain.
Powdery mildew (oidium)White-grey powder on leaves, shoots and berries; berries may split. Likes warm, shady, humid canopies, even without rain.
Botrytis (grey rot / bunch rot)Soft, brown berries covered with grey, furry mould, often near harvest after rain, especially in tight bunches.
Phomopsis (dead arm)Small black spots and cracks on shoots and leaf stalks in spring.
Trunk diseases (such as Eutypa)Dead arms, stunted shoots, dark wedges inside the wood when cut. Enter through pruning wounds.

Viruses

Leafroll virus is common in South Africa. In red cultivars the leaves turn red between the veins and roll downwards in autumn. In white cultivars the leaves turn yellow and roll. Infected vines ripen poorly. Viruses are spread by infected plant material and by mealybugs. There is no cure; infected vines may be marked and removed.

How diseases are controlled

  • Good canopy management so leaves and bunches dry quickly.
  • A spray programme with registered fungicides, applied by trained operators.
  • Removing infected material, as instructed.
  • Planting certified, virus-free vines.
  • Cleaning pruning tools when the farm asks, and protecting large pruning wounds.

lessons.title: Pests and abnormalities
lessons.html:
Pests and abnormalities

Common pests

  • Mealybug: small, white, waxy insects under bark and in bunches. They make sticky honeydew, on which black sooty mould grows. They spread leafroll virus. Ants protect mealybugs, so ant control is part of the plan.
  • Phylloxera: a tiny insect that attacks roots. It is controlled by planting vines on resistant rootstocks.
  • Snout beetle: eats buds and young shoots at night in spring. Workers may find them on the trunk.
  • Bollworm and other caterpillars: eat berries and make holes that let in rot.
  • Mites: very small; leaves may turn bronze, blistered or distorted.
  • Birds, baboons, porcupines and buck: eat grapes or damage vines.
  • Nematodes: tiny worms in the soil that damage roots.

Abnormalities (not caused by pests or disease)

ProblemCause
Sunburnt, brown, shrivelled berries on one sideToo much hot sun after leaf removal or a heat wave
Poor berry set, many small berriesCold, wind or rain at flowering; nutrient shortage such as boron
Split berriesHeavy rain or irrigation on ripe grapes
Hail damageTorn leaves, bruised berries and wounds on shoots
Frost damageYoung shoots turn black and die in spring
Herbicide damageDistorted, cupped or yellow leaves after spray drift
Yellow leavesWater-logging, drought or nutrient shortage

Scouting and reporting

  1. Walk the rows as instructed and look at leaves (both sides), shoots, bunches and trunks.
  2. Note the block, row and what you see.
  3. Report to your supervisor the same day.

Safety with sprays

Pesticides are registered under Act 36 of 1947 and are applied only by trained workers following the label. Never enter a sprayed block before the re-entry time on the label has passed and your supervisor says it is safe.

Key points

  • Downy mildew, powdery mildew and botrytis are major fungal diseases, worse in damp, crowded canopies.
  • Leafroll virus spreads with infected plants and mealybugs; there is no cure.
  • Main pests include mealybug, phylloxera, snout beetle, caterpillars, mites and birds.
  • Sunburn, frost, hail, poor set and spray drift are abnormalities, not diseases.
  • Scout carefully, record the place and report problems quickly.
